English: Nandi intensifies fight against gender violence following alarming statistics. Nandi County has intensified efforts to combat Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and femicide following revelations that 38.4 per cent of women aged between 15 and 49 years have experienced physical violence at some point in their lives, placing the county fifth nationally in the prevalence of physical violence against women. The statistics, released during a sensitisation meeting of the Nandi County Gender Sector Working Group in Kapsabet, have prompted stakeholders to call for urgent, coordinated interventions involving the National Government, County Government, religious institutions, civil society organisations, community leaders and residents. According to the findings presented during the meeting, Nandi ranks behind Kakamega, Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo Marakwet and Vihiga counties in reported cases of physical violence against women. The county also recorded 16 reported femicide cases in 2023, ranking sixth nationally, while 20 cases were reported in 2024, placing it tenth nationally. Participants said the statistics highlight the need for strengthened prevention strategies, improved survivor support services and greater public awareness to curb the rising cases of violence against women and girls. Nandi County Commissioner Wilberforce Kilonzo said addressing GBV and femicide requires collective responsibility and sustained public engagement, noting that government agencies alone cannot eliminate the vice. He said the National Government has continued to use Huduma Mashinani forums across the county’s six sub-counties to educate residents on Gender-Based Violence, teenage pregnancy, child protection and other social challenges affecting communities. Kilonzo urged government agencies, faith-based organisations, civil society groups, schools and community leaders to intensify public awareness campaigns to encourage victims to report cases promptly and help transform attitudes that perpetuate violence. “The fight against Gender-Based Violence requires the active participation of every stakeholder. Through Huduma Mashinani forums, we are continuously sensitising communities on GBV, teenage pregnancy and other social issues, but more partnerships are needed if we are to eliminate these crimes,” he said. County Director of Gender George Ondonga said the meeting was convened to familiarise members of the Gender Sector Working Group with the findings and recommendations of the Gender Technical Working Group on GBV and Femicide and to develop interventions tailored to the county’s needs. Ondonga challenged members of the working group to move beyond policy discussions and become ambassadors against GBV within their respective institutions and communities. “Every member of the Gender Sector Working Group has a responsibility to become an ambassador in the fight against GBV and femicide by taking prevention messages to the grassroots,” he said. Teenage pregnancy also emerged as a major concern during the meeting. Stakeholders heard that 17 per cent of girls aged between 15 and 19 years in Nandi County have experienced pregnancy, with Aldai Sub-county recording the highest prevalence at 23 per cent. Participants said teenage pregnancy, school dropout, harmful cultural practices, alcohol and substance abuse and sexual violence are interconnected challenges requiring integrated interventions involving parents, schools, health providers and community leaders. To strengthen prevention and response, stakeholders recommended increased funding for GBV programmes, expanded public sensitisation campaigns and stronger collaboration among government institutions, faith-based organisations, civil society and community structures. They further proposed convening a county summit bringing together the Council of Elders, senior religious leaders, elected leaders and civil society organisations to develop a unified strategy for combating GBV and femicide. The meeting also resolved to mobilise resources from both the National and County Governments for the construction of a Gender-Based Violence Recovery Centre at Kapsabet County Referral Hospital. Kilonzo and Ondonga committed to convening a consultative meeting with relevant leaders and partners to explore funding options for the proposed facility. The planned recovery centre would provide temporary shelter, psychosocial counselling, legal assistance, medical care and referral services for survivors, particularly those who may face further danger if they return home immediately after reporting abuse. Stakeholders urged the National Government to prioritise Nandi County in its plan to establish a GBV Recovery Centre in every county, citing the county’s high prevalence of physical violence and increasing femicide cases. The meeting also examined the role of cultural practices in shaping behaviour among young people. Participants called on community elders to review the teachings offered during initiation ceremonies to ensure they promote respect for parents, teachers, women and children while discouraging violence, discrimination and harmful cultural norms. They observed that initiation rites should reinforce positive values, responsibility and peaceful coexistence instead of perpetuating attitudes that encourage abuse or gender inequality. Schools and colleges were identified as critical platforms for preventing GBV through education and early intervention. Stakeholders recommended integrating anti-GBV sensitisation programmes into learning institutions by involving teachers, counsellors and peer educators while using digital platforms, videos and other educational materials to create awareness among learners. Recognising the importance of engaging men and boys in preventing violence, the meeting proposed establishing male engagement committees at county and sub-county levels to champion positive masculinity and support community awareness campaigns. Participants also resolved to strengthen GBV referral pathways, improve coordination among duty bearers involved in prevention, reporting and case management, and promote the use of social media to reach more people with anti-GBV messages. They discouraged the use of Kipkaa, a traditional alternative dispute resolution mechanism, to handle GBV cases, saying criminal offences should be reported to law enforcement agencies and prosecuted through the justice system. The meeting further recommended holding standalone anti-GBV public barazas to provide sufficient time for focused discussions on prevention, survivor support and available reporting mechanisms. Stakeholders urged members of the public to report cases of sexual and gender-based violence promptly and called for a harmonised reporting system to improve coordination among government agencies and ensure survivors receive timely assistance. The sensitisation meeting brought together 20 members of the Nandi County Gender Sector Working Group drawn from the National Government Administration, Kenya Police Service, Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action, faith-based organisations and other partner institutions. The participants concluded by reaffirming their commitment to strengthening prevention, survivor protection, public awareness, coordination and accountability in the fight against Gender-Based Violence and femicide, expressing optimism that sustained collaboration among all stakeholders would help reverse the alarming trends and create safer communities across Nandi County. By Geoffrey Satia

English: Groundnut business sustains Kericho trader’s family. As formal employment opportunities remain limited, many Kenyans are increasingly turning to Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to earn a living, support their families and contribute to local economic growth. Across towns and trading centres, small businesses continue to provide livelihoods for thousands of entrepreneurs, proving that modest investments, combined with determination and hard work, can transform lives and create sustainable sources of income. For 45-year-old Daniel Langat, a groundnut trader operating in Kericho town, selling roasted groundnuts has become more than just a business. It is the enterprise that has sustained his family, educated his children and given him hope for a better future over the past decade. Originally from Olenguruone in Kuresoi South Constituency, Nakuru County, Langat runs his business near the Jumbo area and opposite Kericho County Referral Hospital, serving commuters, traders, patients, visitors and residents throughout the day. The father of five says the business has enabled him to meet household expenses, pay rent and educate his children, with his first-born expected to complete Form Four this year. Langat’s entrepreneurial journey began after financial challenges forced him to drop out of school after completing Class Eight. Unable to continue with his education because his family could not afford school fees, he ventured into various informal jobs in search of a reliable source of income. Before settling on groundnut trading, he sold pineapples, hawked soap and worked for other people while learning the basics of running a business. From those experiences, he realised that roasted groundnuts offered a more dependable market. Compared to some of the other products he had sold, customers rarely complained about quality, while demand remained relatively steady throughout the year. Nearly 10 years later, the business has grown into his family’s main source of livelihood. Langat sells roasted groundnuts in packages ranging from Sh10 to Sh50 and above, making the product affordable to customers from different income groups. On slow business days, he earns between Sh1,500 and Sh2,000, while on good days his earnings exceed Sh3,000. He attributes his progress to consistency, discipline and patience rather than the size of his business. “Many people believe success only comes from big businesses, but I have learnt that consistency is more important than size. Every packet I sell brings me a step closer to my goals, and that is what keeps me going despite the daily challenges,” said Langat. Despite the gains, he acknowledges that operating a small business comes with uncertainties. Customer numbers fluctuate from one day to another, making it difficult to predict daily income. He says some days record brisk sales while others attract only a handful of customers, requiring resilience and careful financial planning to remain in business. “Business has its ups and downs. There are days when customers are few and sales are low, but giving up has never crossed my mind. Every new day presents another opportunity, and I have learnt that persistence is what keeps a business alive,” he added. Langat is also an active member of Africa Gospel Church (AGC) Immanuel in Kericho town, where he draws encouragement to remain focused on his business and family responsibilities. Looking ahead, he hopes to expand the enterprise through increased savings and eventually diversify into other income-generating ventures to improve his family’s living standards. He believes access to affordable financing would enable many small-scale traders to increase stock, improve their businesses and create employment opportunities for others. Langat has appealed to the government to establish more designated trading spaces for small-scale entrepreneurs and expand access to affordable loans and grants to help traders grow their enterprises. He further urged the government to introduce empowerment programmes targeting entrepreneurs above the youth age bracket, noting that while several initiatives support young people, many older business owners also struggle to access affordable capital despite operating viable enterprises. According to Langat, strengthening MSMEs through financial support, training and better trading infrastructure would not only improve household incomes but also contribute significantly to local economic development. He also encouraged aspiring entrepreneurs not to wait indefinitely for formal employment but to take advantage of available opportunities, however small, while remaining committed to disciplined financial management. “No work is too small if it is honest. Start with the little capital you have, remain disciplined and save consistently. Do not underestimate any business because what matters is how you organise and manage it. With patience, commitment and wise planning, a small enterprise can grow into a business that supports a family and even creates jobs for others,” he said. As more Kenyans embrace self-employment, MSMEs continue to play a vital role in reducing unemployment and strengthening local economies. Businesses such as Langat’s demonstrate how resilience, prudent management and determination can turn small ventures into reliable sources of income, supporting families while contributing to economic growth and community development. By Faith Chelang’at and Monica Irua

Youth group turns one motorbike into thriving economic venture. A youth group in Ndhiwa East Sub-County has been hailed as a model of economic empowerment after transforming a single motorcycle into a diversified income-generating enterprise that now benefits dozens of its members. The Pala Moyie Boda Boda Youth Group received a major boost in 2018 when the then Ndhiwa MP, Augustino Neto Oyugi, donated one motorcycle to each of 22 youth groups under a youth economic empowerment programme. The group was among the beneficiaries. Speaking at Ojode Pala Trading Centre in South Kabuoch Location during a goat handover ceremony, the group’s Executive Secretary, Mark Onyango, said proceeds from the motorcycle business enabled the members to invest in three tents and a set of chairs, which they now hire out for community events such as weddings, funerals and meetings. The group later accumulated savings of about Sh268,000, allowing it to expand its investments. This week, members purchased 53 female goats and distributed them to 53 members as part of a livestock-rearing project aimed at improving household incomes. “While purchasing the goats, we could not get enough animals for all our members. We will later purchase the remaining 17 she-goats so that every member benefits from the initiative,” Onyango said. The former Ndhiwa MP, Augustino Neto Oyugi, who is also the co-party leader of the United Green Movement (UGM), praised the group’s prudent management of the resources they received. “When I first donated the motorbikes in 2018, I encouraged the 22 youth groups beneficiaries to use them to generate income. This particular group saved about Sh268,000 and invested in tents and chairs. They have now moved beyond collective investments to building the economic capacity of individual members by purchasing she-goats,” he said. Oyugi described the initiative as a significant milestone in youth empowerment and pledged continued support for the group. “This is a step in the right direction. We will continue working together with the group to ensure it has greater capacity to grow. We have also supported them with another motorcycle,” he said. He noted that youth empowerment and employment remain key pillars of the United Green Movement Party, adding that Kenya’s youthful population presents both an opportunity and a challenge. “Kenya has a youth demographic dividend, with nearly 70 per cent of the population aged between 18 and 35 years. Youth unemployment remains a serious challenge that requires all stakeholders to work together to address,” he said. Oyugi urged leaders across the country to invest in empowering young people instead of exploiting them for political violence. “Goonism is increasing because many young people are unemployed. As leaders, we must reject the use of youths for such vices and instead empower them with sustainable sources of income so they can live dignified lives,” he added. United Green Movement Party (UGMP) Co-organizing Secretary and Homa Bay County Woman Representative aspirant Elizabeth Ogweno commended the Pala Moyie Boda Boda Youth Group for discipline and resilience. “The Pala Moyie group has demonstrated discipline in management and resilience in the face of challenges. As leaders, we are committed to supporting development-oriented youth groups that are focused on improving the livelihoods of their members,” she said. By Sitna Omar

Kapsabet gears up for Bishop Lelei installation. By L, KNA The Catholic faithful in Nandi are preparing for three days of prayer, ahead of the impending installation of Bishop John Kiplimo Lelei. The cleric is first Bishop of the newly created Kapsabet Diocese and the historic occasion has been scheduled for August 29 to 31. The festivities will open on 29th with a grand procession and vigil prayers at the Kapsabet Catholic Church. Choirs, youth groups, and women’s guilds will lead praise and worship sessions, as thousands gather to spiritually prepare for the ordination. The second day, will be the highlight, when Bishop Lelei is ordained and officially installed during a solemn Holy Mass at Eliud Kipchoge Sports complex in Kapsabet town. The mass will be presided over by the Apostolic Nuncio to Kenya Hurbertus Maria van Megen alongside the Archbishop of Eldoret Rev. Dominic Kimengich and bishops from across the country. The event is expected to attract thousands of Christians, clergy and leaders. On August 31, the faithful will conclude the celebrations with a thanksgiving service and cultural extravaganza, featuring traditional Nandi dances, youth choirs, and musical performances at St. Peters Catholic church in Kapsabet town. Leaders have pledged to support the new diocese both spiritually and socially. During a fundraising Mass on Sunday at Kapsabet Catholic Church, National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula called for unity ahead of the historic installation. “The installation of Bishop Lelei is not just for Catholics; it is a blessing for the whole community. We call on everyone leaders and faithful alike to support the Diocese so that it may grow strong from the very beginning,” he said. The national assembly speaker commended the faithful for their perseverance and commitment saying, the creation of the Kapsabet Diocese is a testimony of faith and endurance. Nandi Governor Stephen Sang described Bishop Lelei’s appointment as a blessing for the County and vowed to fully support the church. “This installation is a unifying milestone for our people and a moment of pride for the entire Nandi community,” he said. Former Cabinet Minister Henry Kosgey, who was among the pioneers advocating for the creation of the new diocese, said the installation was the fruit of long prayers and persistence. “For decades, we petitioned the Vatican for a Diocese in Kapsabet. Today, our prayers have been answered, and future generations will benefit from a stronger presence of the church,” he said. Nandi Woman Rep Cynthia Muge lauded the moment as historic for women and youth. “The new diocese means more opportunities for our young people and women, who are the backbone of the church. Bishop Lelei’s leadership will ensure no one is left behind,” she said. Nandi Deputy Governor Dr. Yulita Mitei echoed the same sentiments, emphasizing inclusivity. “This Diocese will be a pillar not just of faith, but of community development. It will uplift families, empower the vulnerable, and give hope to generations,” added Mitei. Patrick Kitur, Moderator of the Eldoret Diocese, described the incoming Bishop as a devoted servant of God. “He has been a pillar of faith for decades, and this appointment is well deserved,” he said. The creation of the Kapsabet Diocese marks a major milestone for Catholics in Nandi and the wider Rift Valley. Until now, the faithful in the region were under the Diocese of Eldoret, which covered a vast geographical area stretching across several counties. The new Diocese will bring services closer to the people, ease pastoral work, and strengthen evangelization at the grassroots. It is also expected to spur the growth of Catholic-sponsored schools, health facilities, and community development projects in Nandi. Joseph Maiyo, a youth leader from Emgwen sub county said, “For a long time, our Diocese was too wide, and youth programs hardly reached us. Now we will have activities closer home that will nurture our talents and faith.” The 66 year old Bishop Lelei was born in Soy and has served the Catholic Church for over two decades. He was ordained in the early 2000s under the Diocese of Eldoret. He holds a Doctorate in Theology, specializing in liturgy, from the University of Vienna. He has served in various pastoral positions like Vicar in Suwerwa and Chepterit, as well as Parish Priest in Yamumbi, Tachasis, Kapcherop, Tindinyo, and Kapsabet He Studied philosophy at St. Augustine’s Senior Seminary (Mabanga) and theology at St. Thomas Aquinas Major Seminary (Nairobi) Lelei is widely respected for his pastoral approach, calm leadership style and commitment to grassroots evangelism and education He is celebrated for his deep liturgical knowledge, service in formation and seminary governance, as well as his pastoral dedication to families and youth. His appointment is seen as a milestone, ushering in localized spiritual leadership and growth in the Nandi region The installation and elevation of the Kapsabet Diocese is being hailed as both a spiritual triumph and a social milestone, with thousands expected to take part in the three-day celebrations.

Archbishop warns youth against political exploitation and violent gangs. The Archbishop of Nairobi, Most Rev. Philip Anyolo, has warned young people against being manipulated by unscrupulous leaders to participate in violence, saying such actions threaten the country’s peace and future. Archbishop Anyolo discouraged the youth from being lured by financial handouts, saying temporary gains cannot provide meaningful solutions to their challenges or help them improve their lives. He cautioned against the growing trend of recruiting young people into violent groups, noting that involvement in criminal activities destroys their future and damages the country’s reputation. “I call upon every young person to be attentive to what is happening in the country. Don’t allow yourselves to be misused. Refuse to be bought and don’t be drafted into harmful groups that spread violence and destruction,” Anyolo said. The Archbishop was speaking on Saturday during the installation of Bishop Peter Kamomoe as the new Bishop of Wote Diocese at Unoa Sports Ground in Wote town, Makueni Sub-County. He challenged the youth to reject the identity associated with criminal gangs, saying being referred to as a goon should not be considered a source of pride. “It is not very beautiful to be called a goon. Do not value the title goonism. It is not a title anybody can treasure; it is a shameful thing. So don’t allow it,” he said. Anyolo called on leaders to provide proper guidance and mentorship to young people to enable them to become responsible citizens who promote peace and peaceful coexistence. He also urged political leaders to be mindful of their public utterances, especially as the country approaches the 2027 General Election, warning that inflammatory statements could trigger violence. “We are heading towards this political situation. I want our politicians to avoid uttering words that can trigger violence,” he said. The Archbishop encouraged young people to embrace integrity, respect for others and lawful conduct while contributing positively to society. He accused some leaders of exploiting vulnerable youth for personal political interests, saying those who encourage violence do not have the welfare of young people or the country at heart. “We appeal to our young people not to allow themselves to be used, misused and abused by unscrupulous leaders who do not mean well for them or for the country we all love,” he said. Anyolo further encouraged participants attending activities at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa to reflect on the value and potential of young people instead of allowing themselves to become instruments of destruction. “Our young people have enormous value. Let them reflect on the good they can do for society instead of the evil they may be forced to inflict on others,” he added. Bishop Kamomoe succeeds Bishop Paul Kariuki, who retired on medical grounds. Speaking during the occasion, Makueni Governor Mutula Kilonzo Jr expressed concern over recent political events, including the violence witnessed during the Ol Kalou parliamentary by-election. Mutula said the emerging trend of political violence was worrying and should be addressed immediately to protect Kenya’s democratic space. He called on Kenyans to respect the right of citizens to freely participate in elections without intimidation or coercion. “We are in a difficult moment. If the photos I saw from Ol Kalou are true, I urge all believers to pray for this country. People need to be allowed to vote without being influenced,” said Mutula. By Patrick Nyakundi

English: TVETs urged to embrace emerging technologies for industrial revolution skills. Kenya’s Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVETS) institutes should embrace modern training approaches and strengthen collaboration with industry, to help the country produce a workforce capable of meeting the demands of a rapidly evolving technological landscape. According to Kenya Industrial Training Institute (KITI) Director Engineer Wabwile Simiyu technological advancement is transforming every sector of the economy, creating new demands for productivity, innovation and efficiency. Engineer Simiyu explained that industries were increasingly adopting advanced technologies in manufacturing, agriculture, logistics and building management systems requiring workers to be versed with up-to-date technical competencies. He said Digitization was rapidly changing the skills-sets needed in diverse fields by virtue that employers were searching for human resources with proficiencies in artificial intelligence, automation, big data and collaborative technologies. “The fourth industrial revolution (4IR) is evolving the physical learning environment, and we need to accommodate and encourage the uptake of digital skills,” he stated. The Director added that there were developments ushering in unprecedented scientific and technological advancements with capabilities to green the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) education ecosystem, adding that the re-engineering was impacting both how traditional markets are operating and the expertise that will enable TVET learners to stay relevant and benefit from fourth industrial revolution (4IR). Speaking during the institute’s public engagement at its main campus in Nakuru Engineer Simiyu pointed out that to create synergy in the wake of greening the education ecosystem, TVET institutions have to adopt digital innovation, adaptive to deliver intended learning outcomes through digital-driven applications delivery to accelerate creation of green jobs. As the pace of digital transformation evolves, the Director said its relevance to investment in new digital technologies for TVETS was inevitable, adding that TVET learning experiences and knowledge sharing could be made more flexible through simulation-based learning techniques. “Adopting the Competency-Based Education and Training (CBET) framework ensures training matches industry standards, providing graduates with in-demand technical and digital proficiencies,” the official elaborated. The Kenya Industrial Training Institute (KITI) is a State vocational and entrepreneurship training center operating under the Ministry of Investments, Trade and Industry. It equips school leavers, artisans, and Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME) employees with practical, hands-on technical and business skills to foster self-employment and industrial growth. The Director challenged TVET instructors to embrace emerging technologies in their pedagogy and to develop skills to enable the youth leverage on the opportunities that come with the fourth and fifth industrial revolution including the jobs of the future thus bridging the skills supply and demand gap. Engineer Simiyu indicated that Kenyan TVETs need to forge robust linkages and connections with manufacturing concerns and service industries as one way of addressing youth underemployment in the labour market. The Director observed that involving industry in the development of technical training curriculum could help to address the shortage of technical skills in the domestic and commercial sector. He said allowing technical institutions to students to spend a large portion of their time in industry will have them gain hands-on experience. “At KITI we are committed to ensuring that training offered to our students is strengthened so that what is coming out is what is required in the industry. The common denominator of industrial economies is that they have invested heavily in education systems that strongly emphasize technical skills,” he assured. As such, he added they have been able to match the growing demand for new skill sets in a fast-evolving economic environment with the appropriate training models. The United Nations Education, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), has identified linkages between TVETS, government and private sector as a driver of an advanced industrial manpower base. While hailing the State for making policy and curriculum changes aimed at providing young TVET students with competitive skills for self-employment and making vocational training more appealing to youth, in order to address the shortage of required skills in the job market, the Director stated that trainees need to spend at least 25 per cent of their time in class and 75 per cent gaining hands-on experience in the localized models. Engineer Simiyu stated that since 2013 when the Technical Vocational Education and Training Act was enacted, the country has made positive strides in creating the right policy and regulatory environment for technical training. He pointed out that this has seen TVET enrolment levels almost double in the past decade, a clear pointer to the pent-up demand for technical vocational training in Kenya. He noted that Increased funding, enhanced regulations and robust communication campaigns by the government have resulted in TVET enrollment growing by nearly 300 per cent since 2013. This, he added, is attributed to, among others, the reforms in the sector that arose from the implementation of the Technical and Vocational Education and Training Act of 2013. The Director indicated that the establishment of a regulatory body: the Technical and Vocational Education and Training Authority (TVETA), and the Curriculum Development Assessment and Certification Council (CDACC) to oversee curriculum development, assessment and certification of programmes among other efforts have led to the development of more relevant, market-driven technical courses that aim to equip young people with employable skills. He said Partnerships with the private sector could address the shortage of skill in the industry particularly the gaps in training between what is coming out of schools and what is needed in the market. The official observed that involving the industry leaders early in the formulation of the curriculum enables them to direct what is needed in training in regard to the evolving technologies and equips the youth with market-driven skills. Further, he said the disconnect between the industry and TVETS had watered down the value of certifications of the graduates from technical institutions owing to skill-gaps when joining the job market. According to the Director the collaboration between technical institutions and industry also provides trainees with on-site mentor training. Engineer Simiyu further called for strengthening collaborative linkages between government and the private sector in driving the TVET agenda in developing specialized short-term practical courses. He noted that the government and private sector can also collaborate in research targeting the changing market environment and consumer trends. Engineer Simiyu observed that this builds a valuable knowledge base that the private sector and government can leverage to improve technical training and solve real economic problems. According to the Director, evidence shows that providing technical skills training alone is not enough to empower young people to find and create jobs. He emphasized that more can be done to prepare young people to enter and excel in the labour market such as equipping them with wholesome skills, basing policies on available evidence and conducting robust communications activities to change attitudes towards TVET careers. He added that TVET programmes should also incorporate Whole Youth Development skills such as entrepreneurship, communication, problem solving, relational skills and time management saying that much of the current TVET curriculum prioritizes students developing technical skills over soft skills. His concerns come at a time when most tertiary colleges and national polytechnics have been converted to universities where more graduates than skilled artisans in crucial areas are being trained. The Director regretted that polytechnics and other technical schools had been killed by converting them into universities, at the same time glorified university education at the expense of the rest of the training institutions. Engineer Simiyu indicated that there is a need for youths to embrace blue as opposed to white collar jobs through training of artisans because labour is scarce in these fields. The official said they were sensitizing Kenyans to encourage their children to undergo training in TVETs courses and other fields, adding that Artisan jobs were not attractive to many because there is a perception they are for primary and secondary school drop outs. The Director said there was however a ray of hope after enhanced investments in TVET education by the state which was also giving out incentives to promote artisan businesses. He further stated that product innovation was happening at a rapid pace that consumers are getting out of touch with the changes. This he said has created the need for certified workers to ensure efficient service delivery. He emphasized that an effective Technical and Vocational Education Training (TVET) system will play a key role in achievement of the big four Government agenda and Vision 2030. Engineer Simiyu informed TVET students that The Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) was now recognizing certificates issued to informally trained artisans and professionals who pass practical tests conducted by various authorities. Under the new arrangement, the Kenya Accountants and Secretaries National Examination Board (KASNEB), Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC), National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) and Curriculum Development, Assessment and Certification Council (CDACC) issues academic certificates based on practical performance as opposed to written examinations. This effectively means that a jua kali trained, tailor, carpenter, mechanic, sculptor or a plumber who has never sat in a formal classroom or Technical Educational and Vocational Training Institutes (TVETS) may be issued with a recognized certificate just as his counterparts who have undergone years of formal training, the official added. This is however subject to condition that one must practically demonstrate that he or she possesses the requisite skills before a relevant examination. Engineer Simiyu argued that the success of Kenya’s growth ambitions hinged on an adequate supply of a critical mass of technical skills. He said in countries such as Japan, China, Germany and the Netherlands, the majority of those graduating from secondary school prefer technical colleges to universities. “Technical colleges, if well-equipped and managed, are actually the bearing of a nation’s economy… these are the hands that do the actual job, conceptualized by professors, engineers, researchers and university scholars,” he pointed out. However, he dismissed the idea that the rise in popularity of technical colleges could be interpreted to mean that university degrees and education are becoming useless. Instead, the Director noted the need for the two to work together to achieve a greater purpose of economic growth. Engineer Simiyu hailed the government for intensified efforts to formally recognize and validate the skills of thousands of Kenyans working in the informal sector through the Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) program. He said the move is a transformative initiative under the Skills Initiative for Africa (SIFA) project. RPL is a process that acknowledges learning acquired through multiple ways and involves identifying, evaluating and validating an individual’s knowledge, skills and attitudes, regardless of where they were acquired. Engineer Simiyu pointed out that the RPL program was timely as only a fraction of Kenyans access formal job skill training through tertiary institutions, while millions gain work skill through on-the-job training. RPL a national program spearheaded by the Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) and the State Department for TVET helps informal-sector workers especially those in the jua-kali sector (such as mechanics, plumbers, electricians, or masons) who possess valuable skills but lack formal academic papers get officially certified thereby bridging the gap between their practical expertise and formal academic credentials. Engineer Simiyu noted that though Kenya’s workforce has demonstrated its potential through skills acquired via apprenticeship, the Jua Kali sector and Technical and Vocational Education (TVET) training institutions, these informally or non-formally obtained skills often go unrecognized limiting their contribution to the labour market and national progress. He observed that millions of Kenyans in the workforce including cosmetologists, plumbers, masons, electricians, welders and landscaping experts among others have honed their skills through apprenticeships and on the job learning method yet majority of these individuals get excluded from the formal job market where certified recognition could significantly enhance their earning potential. The RPL unit operates in close collaboration with the Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA), the TVET Authority (TVETA), and the Technical and Vocational Education and Training Curriculum Development, Assessment and Certification Council (CDACC) to ensure assessments align with national educational. Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) can be assessed and certified by National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) or at all accredited National Polytechnics, public universities, and registered Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutes across Kenya. Candidates undergo a practical or oral assessment and once verified, they receive an official qualification that is recorded on the Kenya National Qualifications Framework (KNQF). Governor Lusaka defends government’s development record. Bungoma Governor Kenneth Lusaka has mounted a spirited defence of President William Ruto’s development record, urging professionals in the county to take the lead in communicating the government’s achievements as the country heads towards the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the Bungoma Professionals Forum at Kibabii University on Saturday, Lusaka said professionals were best placed to objectively assess the government’s performance based on projects implemented over the past four years rather than political rhetoric. Lusaka said his interactions with the national government over the last four years had given him first-hand knowledge of the progress made in implementing development programmes in Bungoma and the wider Western region. “I have worked closely with this administration in negotiating for Bungoma’s development priorities, and I have seen project after project move from the drawing board to implementation,” he said. The governor said reforms in the sugar industry had begun reversing years of decline by settling historical debts owed to farmers, restructuring sugar factories and attracting private investment. He cited the revival of Nzoia Sugar Company as one of the government’s notable achievements, saying the factory was operating more efficiently following the installation of a new milling machine. “I visited Nzoia Sugar recently and the new milling machine promised by the President is fully operational. The challenge today is no longer low production but finding markets for more than 250,000 bags of sugar currently in storage,” he said. He said the fertiliser subsidy programme had enabled farmers to access inputs directly, eliminating middlemen who had long exploited growers, while coffee and tea farmers were now receiving better returns through direct payments. The governor also outlined major national government projects currently underway in Bungoma, saying they were laying the foundation for long-term economic growth. He said procurement for the expansion of Matulo Airstrip, including construction of a new passenger terminal and extension of the runway, had been completed and the contract would be awarded next week before construction begins. Lusaka further highlighted the construction of modern markets in Chwele, Sirisia, Mbakalo, Matisi and Lwandanyi, saying the facilities would provide improved trading spaces for farmers and small-scale traders. He said work was progressing on key roads, including the Musikoma-Sango-Napakhalo Road and the Turbo-Ekero-Ndalu Road, while the Kimilili-Kamukuywa Road project was set to commence after the award of the construction tender. Other flagship projects, he said, include the Kanduyi Smart City, the Affordable Housing Programme, rural electrification, the implementation of the Social Health Authority (SHA), the upgrade of Masinde Muliro Stadium and the proposed Standard Gauge Railway route through Bungoma. While acknowledging that some projects were still under construction, Lusaka maintained that implementation was on course. “I will not claim that every project is complete, but I can confidently say contractors are on site, procurement has been concluded and implementation is progressing satisfactorily,” he said. The governor also praised the national government’s improved disbursement of funds to counties, saying devolved units had for the first time ended the financial year with all their allocations fully released. “We closed the financial year with all the money due to counties already in our accounts. That has never happened before because counties were previously forced to wait for months for disbursements,” he said. Lusaka acknowledged that the Kenya Kwanza administration assumed office amid rising public debt, prolonged drought and global economic shocks but argued that it had sustained investment in infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare and social services despite the challenges. He challenged professionals to use their expertise and influence to explain government programmes to the public and counter misinformation. “The projects are visible and are transforming lives. President Ruto deserves another term to complete the programmes already underway,” Lusaka said. Speaking at the same forum, Industry Principal Secretary Dr. Juma Mukhwana said no administration since Independence had invested in Bungoma and the wider Western region as heavily as President Ruto’s government. He said the President had also appointed more leaders from Bungoma and the Western region to senior positions in government than previous administrations, demonstrating his commitment to inclusive leadership. “The projects being rolled out by the government are impactful and will significantly spur economic growth in this region. Professionals should take stock of these developments and help inform the electorate about what has been achieved,” said Mukhwana. Mining Principal Secretary Harry Kimtai urged professionals to support the government’s development agenda by helping dispel misinformation and ensuring residents receive accurate information on ongoing projects and programmes. “Professionals have a responsibility to demystify facts and counter misinformation so that wananchi understand exactly what the government is doing,” Kimtai said. Public Service Principal Secretary Dr. Jane Imbunya said the government had ensured development opportunities were distributed equitably across the country regardless of region. She said the government was also strengthening bilateral relations with other countries to create employment opportunities for Kenyan youth through labour mobility programmes. “The government has secured opportunities including scholarships, fellowships and overseas jobs targeting professionals and young people. I urge eligible Kenyans to take advantage of these opportunities by applying,” she said. Tourism Principal Secretary Prof Julius Bitok said every region had benefited from national government projects since President Ruto assumed office. “When I served as Immigration Principal Secretary, I facilitated the establishment of a passport office in Bungoma. Now, at the Ministry of Tourism, we are exploring several projects that the government will invest in to unlock the county’s tourism potential,” he said. Bitok urged professionals to rally behind President Ruto’s re-election bid, saying continuity would ensure the completion of ongoing development projects and programmes across Bungoma and the country. Daycare initiative gives young mothers second chance at education. A daycare programme established at a vocational training centre in Mathioya Constituency, Murang’a County, is enabling young mothers to return to school by providing safe childcare services while they pursue skills training. The initiative, introduced by the 360 Climate Institute, is helping teenage mothers rebuild their lives after pregnancies interrupted their education, allowing them to balance motherhood and learning without compromising the wellbeing of their children. At the centre of the programme is the“Cha Mama” Daycare Baby Crèche, where trained caregivers look after infants and toddlers from morning until evening as their mothers attend classes. The arrangement allows learners to concentrate on their studies while remaining close enough to breastfeed and check on their children during breaks. The programme was established in response to the growing number of young women who wanted to resume education but lacked reliable childcare support. For many beneficiaries, the initiative has become a pathway to restoring confidence, acquiring employable skills and securing a better future for themselves and their children. Jane Njeri, a beneficiary from Nyandarua County, said the programme enabled her to continue pursuing a catering course after giving birth. She explained that she enrolled at the institution while pregnant and took maternity leave before returning to complete her training with the support of the daycare facility. “I first learnt about this school online, applied and joined to study catering. At the time I was pregnant,” she said. Njeri noted that balancing exclusive breastfeeding with coursework has not been easy but said the daycare has made it possible for her to continue learning without neglecting her child. She expressed gratitude to the institution for creating an environment that allows young mothers to pursue education while fulfilling their parental responsibilities. Another beneficiary, Jane Wanjiru, has progressed from being one of the programme’s first students to becoming a trainer at the institution. She described the initiative as a turning point that transformed what once seemed like the end of her education into an opportunity for personal and professional growth. “I am a trainer and a beneficiary of the daycare centre. I would not be able to work without the daycare because it helps me juggle work and motherhood,” she said. Wanjiru encouraged other young mothers who had abandoned education after becoming pregnant to take advantage of similar opportunities and work towards rebuilding their futures. The success of the programme has also been attributed to caregivers such as Nancy Gakii, who ensures children are well-fed, safe and cared for throughout the day. Her work enables mothers to attend lessons with confidence, knowing their children are receiving proper care in a secure environment. The initiative has received positive support from members of the local community, who say it is helping reduce the stigma often associated with teenage motherhood. Resident Susan Wangui said many parents are unable to care for their daughters’ children during the day because they also have to work to support their families. “We have girls who dropped out of school after getting pregnant and sometimes, as parents, we cannot help with childcare because we also have to work the whole day,” she said. Joseph Gikungu welcomed the programme, saying it restores hope to young mothers who would otherwise struggle to return to school. “Allowing young mothers to come to school with their children makes me happy because it gives them hope,” he said. According to the Chief Executive Officer of the 360 Climate Institute, Daniel Irungu, the initiative was launched in 2024 after the organisation identified a growing need among young mothers seeking vocational training. “We realised there was a gap in society when we saw many young mothers who wanted skills but had no one to take care of their young children,” he said. Irungu said early parenthood should not mark the end of a young woman’s education or career aspirations, adding that access to skills training can help young mothers achieve financial independence. The institute’s founder and Board Chairperson, Hannah Muriithi, said the idea was inspired by the determination shown by young mothers who wanted to learn but were held back by childcare responsibilities. “We created a safe space where babies can play, learn and remain secure while their mothers attend training or teach different skills,” she said. Muriithi appealed to development partners, well-wishers and other organisations to support the programme so that more young mothers can benefit from vocational education and childcare services. She said expanding the initiative would enable more girls who dropped out of school due to pregnancy to acquire practical skills, improve their livelihoods and become economically self-reliant. The programme has emerged as a model of how targeted support can help young mothers overcome barriers to education, demonstrating that with access to childcare, skills training and community support, they can successfully balance motherhood and learning while creating brighter futures for themselves and their children. By Purity Mugo

English: Researchers identify solutions to reduce pesticide residues on farm produce. Did you know that the simple act of soaking your fresh leafy spinach in salty water, then washing them under running water before cooking them could be the difference between living longer or dying earlier? A report by the Kenya Organic Agriculture Network (KOAN), in partnership with the Route to Food Initiative (RTIFI) and the Heinrich Böll Foundation (HBF) has demonstrated that these rudimentary practices can reduce the average detectable pesticide residue by 72.4 %. The joint report titledPesticide Residues in Selected Vegetables from Kenyan markets and Effectiveness of Household Methods for Residue Reductionlists a total of eight simple home practices that have been found to effectively address the challenge of pesticide residues in foods commonly consumed by majority of Kenyans on a daily basis. During the study, four vegetable varieties namely bulb onions, kales, spinach and tomatoes were employed under the study. The 45 samples used in the study were sourced from various markets in Nairobi and Nakuru cities. The markets were selected since most of their fresh produce are sourced from upcountry farms in Nyeri, Nyandarua, Machakos, Kirinyaga and Kajiado counties. “On average, soaking(vegetables) in salty water, washing under running water plus cooking gave the highest average reduction at 72.4 %; this was followed by washing in running water plus blanching at 70 %, then soaking in baking soda water plus washing and cooking had 69.8 %, while soaking in baking soda, washing plus cooking had 69.8 % reduction. This was followed by vinegar at 64.6 %, washing under running water at an average reduction of 61 %, and lastly, a 56.6% reduction was achieved with soaking in baking soda plus washing under running water,” read the report released on July 19, 2026 at the Central Bank of Kenya Institute of Monetary Studies during a stakeholders’ forum dubbed Food Safety in Kenya:From Evidence to Action. From the study onions exhibited the best pesticide reduction rate with all seven treatment methods within a range of between 98.7% and 99.7%. Tomatoes came second with a high of 68.3 % residue reduction rate after being soaked in baking soda followed by washing under running water before cooking. Spinach came third at 65.5 % after soaking in salty water then washing under running water and later cooking. On the other hand, soaking kales in vinegar, washing them under running water and finally cooking them achieved a 62.3% reduction in residues. The report also revealed that 78 % of the samples tested during the study had detectable pesticides while a third had surpassed EU Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs). MRLs is the maximum concentration of a pesticide residue on food or feed of plant and animal origin that is legally tolerated. The pesticides detected above EU MRLs comprised fungicides, insecticides, an herbicide and a miticide, laying bare the diversity of pesticide products farmers employ in vegetable husbandry. Tomatoes carried the highest burden, accounting for two-thirds of the non-compliant samples while onions came relatively clear. The report also found that household preparation methods can reduce pesticide residues by 60 to 70 %. “Food safety is everyone’s responsibility. This dialogue brings together evidence, experience and diverse voices to identify practical actions that can strengthen Kenya’s food system, from the farm to the consumer’s table, alongside data on pesticide residue reduction levels,” said Eustace Kiare, KOAN Executive Director during the release of the findings at the In 2024, a baseline study in Nyeri, Meru, Kirinyaga, Taita Taveta and Makueni counties on kales, tomatoes and onions by the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) showed that out of 105 samples, 33 (31 %) had pesticide residues exceeding the EU-MRLs. The report further noted that previous pesticide monitoring researches had demonstrated that a proportion of vegetables being consumed in the country contain pesticide that exceed internationally recognized MRLs. KOAN is therefore calling for routine surveillance of pesticides in order to provide scientific evidence for evaluating compliance with pesticide regulations, assessing consumer exposure and informing national food safety policies. “Such information is particularly relevant in settings where consumers rely primarily on domestic food preparation to minimize dietary exposure. The results are expected to benefit regulatory agencies, public health practitioners, agricultural extension services, researchers, development partners, and consumers by providing evidence that supports safer agricultural production and healthier food preparation practices,” the report explains. According to a 2024 joint report by PCPB and FAO, Kenya’s pesticide imports rose from 14,600 tons in 2015 to 19,932 metric tons by 2020, catalyzed by a growing agricultural production and market demand. Another report in 2022 showed that 76 % of the total volume of pesticides used in Kenya contained or more active ingredients that are labelled as Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHPs). Both WHO and FAO identify HHPs in pesticides based on their toxicity to human health, persistence in the environment and toxicity to aquatic life and pollinators. The report therefore insists that though the samples from the study exhibited pesticide residue below regulatory limits, excessive or repeated dietary exposure to certain pesticides has in the past been associated with adverse health outcomes. “Acute exposure (to pesticides) may cause symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, skin irritation, and respiratory distress, whereas long-term exposure has been linked to neurological disorders, endocrine disruption, reproductive impairment, developmental abnormalities and increased risks of cancers,” reads the findings. “Consequently, routine surveillance of pesticide residues remains an important component of national food safety systems.” Dr Harun Warui, RTFI programme Coordinator says Kenya lacks a single fix to address the challenge of harmful pesticides on human food and requires all stakeholders on board to find a way around the problem. Dr Warui argued that Kenya should not rely on policies in order to cut down on use of pesticides but should instead come up with less hazardous pest control practices that do not imperil both man and environment. “Today’s launch offers households a practical way to cut down pesticide exposure, but it cannot stand alone as the fix. The evidence keeps pointing in the same direction: without stronger regulation, unsafe food linked to highly hazardous pesticides will keep reaching consumers,” said Dr Warui. “We need a 360-degree approach, one that pairs household action with firmer enforcement of pesticide standards, so that safety does not depend on what happens in the kitchen alone. Agroecology gives us a further route to the same goal, growing food in ways that reduce our reliance on hazardous pesticides in the first place, rather than only managing their residues after the fact.” Dr Johnson Nduhiu Gitahi, a staff at the Nairobi University Department of Public Health, Pharmacology and Toxicology explained the need of the entire study was to explore practical solutions to safer foods in Kenya. Dr Gitahi said all those involved in the entire food chain must make sure what is grown in the farms is safe for the kitchen before it finds its way to the dining table. “Our goal was to provide evidence that people can use every day. Safer food starts on the farm, but simple steps at home can also help reduce pesticide residues before vegetables are eaten,” he stated. Early this year eight non-governmental organizations drawn from East Africa had called for concrete policies to help safeguard both man and environment from effects of HHPs. In a joint statement released on March 27 this year, the group under the umbrella of East Africa Pesticide Network had noted the steps the region had taken in reducing the usage of hazardous pesticides but warned findings showed there was still presence of HHPs in the ecosystem. The network had brought together Greenpeace Africa, RTFI, Food Safety Coalition Uganda, Global Consumer Center, Broederlijk Delen, SEATINI, Tanzania Organic Agricultural Movement and Premium Kenya. The report followed findings that were presented during the East Africa Pesticides, Environment and Health Interdisciplinary Symposium held in Kisumu from November 5 to 6 2025. The group wanted the region to come up with strong enforcement, transparent registration processes, and regular monitoring and publication of data on pesticide reduction. In addition, they wanted governments from the East Africa region to develop an effective surveillance of acute and chronic pesticide poisoning and coordinated regional action to prevent cross-border pesticide trade in hazardous products. “At the policy level, we recognize that important regulatory steps are already being taken to protect our health and the environment, as well as transboundary control of hazardous products. In June 2025, Kenya announced the withdrawal of 77 per cent of products and restrictions on an additional 202. Earlier this year, Tanzania announced the phase-out of 805 products, a step that demonstrates the growing recognition of pesticide risks. These actions signal growing recognition of the risks posed by pesticides; however, regulatory bans alone are not enough.” read the statement. According to the report, global pesticide uses in East Africa rose from 1.8 million tons to 3.7 million tons between 1990 and 2022, posing a challenge in tackling entry of harmful chemicals into the region. On the other hand, pesticide imports into Africa increased 5.7 times between 2002 and 2022, a pointer to broader agricultural intensification trends driven by changing climatic patterns, pest pressure and food production demands. During the same period, pesticide used on food crops exceeded the allowed safety limits posing health risks to both humans and the environment. “Today, we present findings of studies shared at the symposium that found pesticide residues in drinking water sources, agricultural soils, fresh produce, and ambient air in parts of East Africa. These effects are as a result of exposure, use and misuse of pesticides products that have already been banned in their countries of origin, but are available and sold in countries in the global south, such as Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania,” continued the report. “In some food samples, pesticide limits exceeded established maximum residual levels (MRLs). Health research also documented cases of acute pesticide poisoning and identified links between occupational pesticide exposure and neurological, mental health, and reproductive outcomes among agricultural workers.” To cut down on use of HHPs in the region, respective governments were advised to among other things adhere to existing international agreements such as the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions which outline regulations on hazardous waste movement and trade. At the regional level, member states were urged to adhere to EAC Guidelines on Data Requirements for the Registration of Conventional Chemical Pesticides Used in Agriculture and Forestry adopted during the 38thExtra –Ordinary Council of Ministers on January 30 2019. The Convection provided applicants with better information on the data and studies on how they should submit to national pesticide registration. “Despite the legal frameworks, there are existential challenges to implementation, corporate control over the food system, and weak negotiation capacity between the EAC and the global north. These have continued to influence the continuous trade in and use of highly hazardous pesticides in the region. East African countries still struggle to coordinate joint actions on the regulation and control of the trade in and use of highly hazardous pesticides. There are still challenges of porous borders where pesticides registered, traded, or used in one country often move across borders through formal and informal markets,” highlighted the report. The East Africa Pesticide Network also called for continuous adoption of viable alternatives such as crop diversification, use of biological control agents, soil health management, habitat management for natural enemies and farmer-led integrated pest management. The group noted that such a paradigm shift has in the past helped reduce chemical dependence while safeguarding the soil ecosystem. The network also called for stronger regional collaborative action involving the governments, farmers, researchers, civil societies among others in pushing for initiatives that will protect the public health, food chain and the environment through adopting safer agricultural production practices. In October 2023 KOAN), Biodiversity and Biosafety Association of Kenya(biba), and RTFI had called stakeholders in the agricultural sector to come up with an effective panacea on the use of HHPs in the country. The trio, while admitting the then efforts which were being undertaken towards protecting the safety of crops in regard to the use of pesticides in the country had argued that such efforts should bring more players on board. “A collaborative effort among regulatory bodies, farmers, environmentalists and civil society is crucial to finding a balanced and sustainable approach to pesticide use, especially concerning the use of Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya,” read a joint press statement from the group. “We agree that the responsible use and handling of pesticides are essential. However, we must acknowledge that the responsibility for safe pesticide use is beyond the farmers’ ability. Required mitigation measures like buffer zones to safeguard communities or water resources often can’t be implemented. Beyond the responsibility of the farmer, pesticide companies should also play an essential role in ensuring the safe use, disposal and handling of their products through extended producer responsibility (EPR).” In September 13 2022, RTFI released a report detailing how the majority of Kenyans could be consuming foods laced with HHPs posing a threat to their overall wellbeing. The reportToxic Business; Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya,identified maize, wheat, coffee, potatoes, kales and tomatoes as consumers of the largest volumes of pesticides heavily laced with HHPs. As a result, the crops which form the bulk of the country’s food sources were said to be exposed to a range of toxic substances, a threat to both consumers and the environment. Further, according to the 40-page report, only six out of 310 pesticides in use in the country at the time could be qualified as bio pesticides (derived from natural materials such as plant and animal products and therefore considered safe), accounting for a paltry 2 per cent of the total pesticide volume. “Common food items in Kenya households such as maize, wheat, coffee, potatoes, kales and tomatoes require the largest volumes of pesticides, with a heavy reliance on HHPs.These crops are exposed to a range of toxic substances, posing significant threats to both consumers and the environment,” read the report’s findings. “Only six out of the 310 pesticide products used in Kenya are bio pesticides, accounting for a mere 2 per cent of the total pesticide volume. Meanwhile, Highly Hazardous Pesticides account for a shocking 76 per cent of the total volume used. This huge disparity indicates the urgent need to promote bio pesticides.”. But responding to the report later, PBCB and aak/GROW Fresh Produce Consortium of Kenya (FPC Kenya) faulted the findings insisting the State had been keen in ensuring pesticides landing in the country do not impair the health of man, beast and environment. The board also clarified that only insecticides that meet the required MRLs were allowed into the country. “Ensuring consumer and pesticide user safety is our top priority. Food safety is key during approval of pesticides that is why Maximum Residue Levels are required,” said PCPB then acting CEO Fredrick Muchiri. “The Route to Food initiative report is not factual. Ban means total ban on manufacture and use. You cannot ban a pesticide and continue producing for other people,” he said. The official similarly defended the use of pesticides in the country saying they do play a crucial role in safeguarding crop production by combating pests and disease-causing agents But KOAN, RTFI and biba claimed there was a need to follow a hazard assessment for registering very toxic pesticides (WHO 1a, WHO 1b, and so-called CMR (carcinogenic, mutagenic and reproduction toxic pesticides)) as a matter of urgency. The NGOs said such hazard assessments should focus on the inherent properties of pesticides, regardless of their use patterns. “It is essential to strike a balance between risk and hazard assessments to ensure comprehensive safety, as many of the Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHP) mentioned in the recently launched report Toxic Business: Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya are very toxic, for example, beta-cyfluthrin. We agree that the responsible use and handling of pesticides are essential.” they pointed out. And in response to PCPB’s stance on importation of pesticides currently flagged in Europe, the NGOs had remarked that the products under question had been outlawed due to their health risk to both humans and the environment. They therefore called for exploration of friendlier means of food production that rely less on agrochemicals and also guarantee bumper harvests and access to safe food for the country. “We encourage PCPB to explore sustainable pest management alternatives that prioritize both crop protection and the long-term health of Kenyan farmers and consumers, and the environment. We would like to emphasize that most of the pesticides that are banned in Europe are withdrawn from the market because of their unacceptable risk towards the environment and human health and not because of less pest pressure.” They stressed. “We would also like to emphasize that a system change of agricultural production is necessary and not just a substitution from one pesticide to the other, to achieve safe food in an enabling environment.” Among pesticides ingredients considered highly toxic and commonly used by farmers in the country by then included chlorpyrifos, acetochlor, glyphosate, 2,4-D, mancozeb and chlorothalonil. Active ingredients, such as bifenthrin, dichlorvos, diazinon, carbaryl, fipronil, Thiamethoxam, and carbendazim, have already been outlawed in Europe. By Samuel Maina
